abstract: This paper examines the health consequences of the rapid increase in antidepressant consumption in Switzerland (2002–2014). Using a shift-share instrumental variable approach, we exploit regional variation in sales driven by product innovation (the shift) and the market power of pharmaceutical firms (the share). Our findings reveal that a one defined daily dose per 1,000 inhabitants increase in antidepressant sales raises hospital admissions for adverse drug reactions by 18% and for depression by 6%. Financial incentives for self-dispensing doctors and reduced access to psychotherapy emerge as key drivers, highlighting concerns about overtreatment and suboptimal prescribing practices.
title: Happy Pills? The Health Consequences of the Dramatic Increase in Antidepressant Use

abstract: Successes and failures often appear to propagate. According to one common belief, the experience of winning or losing can alter the cognitive and emotional state of performers, generating a psychological momentum that helps or harms subsequent performance. This belief is often used to rationalize the so-called hot-hand phenomenon, and has been applied to contexts ranging from horseshoe pitching to stock market trading. However, the existence of a causal effect of winning on subsequent performance remains debated. I test whether wins cause more wins (and losses more losses) using a large natural experiment involving almost a quarter billion online chess games. I find that performance is serially correlated, consistent with the existence of hot hands. Surprisingly, however, I find no evidence of causal effects. Players that were given a small random advantage in one game have no advantage in the next. The null effect is precisely estimated, providing credible evidence against the hypothesis that success breeds success in online chess.
title: Tilting at Windmills: Evidence on Momentum and Hot Hands

abstract: This study investigates the role of long‐term population relatedness in shaping global variation in state capacity. It argues that longer periods of ancestral separation are associated with greater divergence in intergenerationally transmitted civic norms governing voluntary compliance with state institutions. Ancestral distance may also hinder the international diffusion of effective state institutions, contributing to persistent cross‐country differences in state capacity. The empirical analysis shows that countries with greater ancestral distance from the global frontier of effective state institutions exhibit lower state capacity. Dyadic regressions further indicate that ancestral distance is associated with greater divergence in state capacity. To examine a potential cultural foundation of this relationship, I exploit variation in cultural backgrounds among second‐generation immigrants residing in the same country. I find that immigrant populations with greater ancestral distance exhibit larger differences in self‐reported attitudes towards voluntary tax compliance. Taken together, the findings suggest that ancestral distance is an important historical predictor of cross‐country disparities in state capacity, consistent with a role for divergence in civic norms and barriers to institutional diffusion.
journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics
title: Ancestral Distance and the Cultural Foundations of State Capacity

abstract: Women's labour force participation features prominently in discussions of low birth rates and the Second Demographic Transition, and has also been hypothesized to have played a role in falling marital fertility during the First Demographic Transition. Historical data have been lacking, however, to assess these theories robustly and to distinguish between the effects of women's work on birth intervals and parity progression. This paper uses a split‐population cure model to analyse stopping and spacing by couples in late‐nineteenth‐century Derbyshire, using linked census data to demonstrate the association between women's occupations before marriage and subsequent marital fertility. Combining these linked census records and the 1911 census fertility survey, complete birth histories have been reconstructed for women who married from the 1880s onwards. The results suggest that couples in this period were controlling their fertility from the beginning of marriage via a combination of stopping and spacing, and that spacing births played a greater role in the low fertility of female textile workers than it did amongst some other occupational groups. These results provide more concrete evidence for the importance of women's labour force participation and birth spacing during the fertility transition in England and Wales.
title: Whether and when: Women's work, birth spacing, and parity progression in late‐nineteenth‐century Derbyshire

abstract: Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced assortative matching between workers and firms, lowered the skill premium, and weakened firms’ monopsony power.
title: Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany

abstract: Gravity models of foreign direct investment have been theoretically justified by supervision costs. Those costs fall when investors understand how the destination's institutions work, which is easier the more they resemble their own. We construct a measure of institutional similarity from Wikipedia's hyperlink network connecting countries. Like investment, our measure is directional. Unlike preexisting indices, it decomposes under one rule into institutional layers. Every layer predicts the probability of positive investment and the size of the position, and jointly they explain more than gravity controls and established institutional indices. We find that similarity pays most when investors have a channel to act on it. Where domestic institutions are weak, that channel may be absent. Between non‐OECD countries without a trade agreement, formal similarity is worth a third of what it is elsewhere, and an agreement closes most of the gap. Such agreements can therefore unlock investment that domestic institutions cannot yet support.
title: Institutional Similarity and Foreign Direct Investment

abstract: This paper uses global mutual funds to study foreign information dissemination across countries into multinationals’ stock prices. To invest internationally, these funds collect information from foreign countries where they invest. Such foreign information helps funds invest in U.S. multinationals operating in those same foreign countries. Global funds overweight and outperform on the selected multinationals’ stocks. They exploit market‐level, industry‐level, and firm‐specific foreign information. The trading activities of these funds accelerate the incorporation of foreign information into the selected multinationals’ prices. Our findings suggest that global mutual funds are important mechanisms for information dissemination into multinationals’ asset prices in global markets.
journal: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking
title: The Added Bonus of Foreign Investments: Global Mutual Funds and Multinational Firm Returns

abstract: This paper analyzes how collateral quality shocks affect banks' liquidity management and the risk‐free rate. We develop a model where banks manage liquidity through near‐cash assets and marketable securities subject to idiosyncratic and/or aggregate shocks. Collateral quality deterioration leads to nonmonotonic changes in liquidity holdings: moderate declines reduce cash holdings via lower market returns, while severe declines cause precautionary hoarding and market freezes. Reduced collateral quality depresses the risk‐free rate. Liquidity regulation and negative interest rate policies can mitigate these effects. Our findings highlight the risks of collateral quality shocks and the importance of policy complementarities in addressing liquidity issues.
journal: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking
title:
Liquidity, Collateral Quality, and Interest Rates

abstract: Abstract Associations between pollution and life expectancy, infant mortality, and cardiorespiratory disease are documented in China. Yet, less is known about environmental drivers of Chinese cancers. Here, we systematically link polluting industrial activity to cancer incidence, cancer mortality, and cancer cluster designations. We investigate county-level associations between industrial production and age-adjusted incidence and mortality reported in official cancer registries. We then combine the locations of roughly 3 million enterprises with administrative data from roughly 600,000 villages and cancer cluster documentation from 380 villages. We show that county-level value-added from industry is associated with age-adjusted incidence and mortality for all cancers; bronchus, trachea, and lung cancers; stomach cancers; and esophageal cancers. We show that the odds that a village contains a documented cancer cluster increase 3-4 times if the village contains a pollution-intensive industrial facility. Leather, chemical, and dye enterprises appear to drive results. All else equal, smaller facilities increase the odds of cancer clusters.

abstract: This paper estimates the impacts of ozone pollution on hospitalizations, medical expenditure, and in-hospital mortality using inpatient admission records from 1,087 hospitals in China between 2017 and 2021. Leveraging an instrumental variable based on ozone concentrations in nearby upwind cities, we find that ozone significantly increases all-cause hospitalizations and medical expenditure. Ozone elevates hospital admissions across a broader range of diseases than previously documented, and the hospitalization cost of 1-standard deviation increase in ozone is larger than that of PM2.5. Ozone reduces the average number of doctors per inpatient and increases the all-cause in-hospital mortality rate in emergency departments, suggesting that ozone-induced surges in healthcare demand generate hospital crowding, which lowers the quality of care and worsens patient outcomes.

abstract: Rising household energy insecurity, more frequent extreme weather events, and growing grid reliability risks put increasing pressure on governments to protect households from energy-related harm. Governments rely on grid reliability standards and safety nets to achieve national energy security goals, protecting the energy system from the top down. But these energy security measures do not extend beyond the meter. Drawing on policy theory and four U.S. energy programs, this policy perspective examines how current U.S. energy policies’ design, purpose, and metrics fail to conceptualize and achieve household energy security. With energy insecurity on the rise, households are unable to meet basic energy needs and are exposed to unsafe indoor temperatures, physical and psychological harm, and increased mortality risk. Structural energy efficiency offers an effective way to improve household energy security by lowering health risks and economic energy insecurity and strengthening passive survivability during outages. But U.S. energy policy continues to justify energy efficiency retrofits in homes primarily as a cost-saving measure, not as an energy security goal, whereas policy measures and costs to improve national energy security are justified by protecting national security. This perspective argues that policy should evaluate structural energy efficiency measures based on whether they provide households with energy security and recommends a local minimum household energy security standard, met at least cost. A minimum standard shifts the question from whether energy efficiency investments pay for themselves to whether homes keep households safe, even when energy systems fail, extending energy security beyond the meter.
title: Extending security beyond the meter: Rethinking energy security and energy efficiency policy at the household level

abstract: Does geopolitical risk impede the energy transition, and can institutional quality mitigate its adverse effects? This study investigates these questions using panel data for 12 selected European Union countries from 2002 to 2024. The study constructs a multidimensional Energy Transition Index (ETI) using principal component analysis (PCA) to capture energy structure, energy efficiency, and energy security. The empirical analysis employs country- and year-fixed-effects models and assesses robustness using Driscoll-Kraay standard errors and panel-corrected standard errors (PCSEs). The specifications account for foreign direct investment, trade openness, urbanization, domestic credit, renewable energy production, carbon emissions, and environmental tax. The findings indicate that geopolitical risk is negatively associated with energy-transition performance, whereas institutional quality is positively associated with it. The positive and statistically significant interaction between geopolitical risk and institutional quality suggests that stronger institutions attenuate the adverse association between geopolitical risk and the energy transition. These findings highlight the importance of institutional capacity and complementary energy, environmental, and investment conditions in sustaining the energy transition amid geopolitical uncertainty.
title: Geopolitical risk and energy transition in the European Union: Can institutional quality mitigate geopolitical shocks?

abstract: The U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) for greenhouse gases (GHG) reduction help protect domestic industries but drive global shifts in the supply chains of electric vehicle batteries. Until now, the effect of these protectionism-based trade policies on GHG emissions in cross-border supply chains has not been quantitatively examined. This study investigates the global impacts of national and regional trade policies on the carbon footprints of batteries from major manufacturing countries. The supply chain scenarios take into account observed and prospective shifts in response to IRA and CBAM-like policies, respectively. The battery carbon footprints are evaluated based on life cycle assessment (LCA). The scenario-based results show that trade policies are overall effective in reducing GHG emissions but the IRA policy paradoxically hinders South Korean and German manufacturers from establishing low-carbon supply chains. Interestingly, the protectionism-based CBAM-like policy could be effectively met by using neoliberalism-based free trade which can globally utilize low-carbon suppliers. The policies could induce carbon leakage beyond the borders of the manufacturing country and affect cross-border emissions. Therefore, international cooperation is required to prevent adverse impacts of policies; globally utilizing low-carbon suppliers is a realistic solution to reduce carbon footprint; and national GHG inventories should be advanced to manage out-of-country emissions.
title: Global impacts of national and regional trade policies on the carbon footprint of electric vehicle battery

abstract: Identifying effective conservation and restoration priorities in agricultural landscapes is a key challenge for environmental governance. While scientific assessments often guide these decisions, local perceptions provide valuable insights into how communities experience environmental change and prioritize ecosystem protection. This study integrates social perceptions with spatial locations to identify socially perceived conservation and restoration priorities among a sample of inhabitants of the Colombian Coffee Region, a biodiversity-rich agricultural landscape facing increasing pressures from land-use change, urban expansion, and tourism development. We applied a mixed-methods approach by analyzing social survey data through frequency analyses and integrating the spatial locations of identified priority areas. Stakeholder interviews complemented the survey results by providing deeper insights into the perspectives of key stakeholders. Survey responses were coded and linked to spatial land-cover categories to assess how perceived priorities are distributed across the landscape. Frequency analyses were used to examine differences in perceptions between urban and rural residents and between landowners and non-landowners. Rivers and associated riparian ecosystems emerged as the most frequently identified priorities for both conservation and restoration, reflecting their central role in water provision and ecosystem functioning. Rural residents and landowners prioritized rivers and forests, whereas urban residents and non-landowners more frequently identified urban ecosystems as priority areas. Spatial analysis revealed substantial overlap between areas perceived as priorities for conservation and restoration. Respondents most frequently identified agriculture, pollution, and urban expansion as environmental threats, while interviews highlighted governance challenges, economic inequality, and poorly regulated tourism as key drivers of environmental degradation. These findings highlight the importance of integrating social perceptions into spatial planning to better align restoration strategies with local priorities and strengthen environmental governance in socio-ecological landscapes.
title: Integrating social perceptions into spatial planning for conservation and restoration in the Colombian Coffee Region

abstract: This letter examines whether an external, multidimensional, high-stakes measure of program quality predicts heterogeneity in the returns to short-cycle tertiary technical education. We use student-level administrative data matched to official program-quality scores and estimate individual fixed-effects models with individual-specific linear time trends. We find that employment, earnings, and skill-match returns to the diploma are lower in low-rated programs. Delving into the different dimensions of the composite quality indicator, we find that program attractiveness and firms’ involvement in traineeships provide the strongest signals, with the traineeship gradient persisting also once controlling for program attractiveness.
title: Dimensions of Program Quality and Returns to Short-Cycle Technical Education

abstract: Liquidity risk remains a persistent threat to financial stability, as starkly demonstrated by the 2023 banking turmoil in the United States and Europe. Hence, the ability to quickly gauge banks’ liquidity risks could prove useful especially during periods of market stress, but also to assess differences in liquidity buffers across peer economies and banks. Yet, publicly available information on banks’ liquidity resilience is patchy: regulatory disclosures are limited in coverage and history, and supervisory liquidity stress tests are typically run by authorities using confidential data. To help fill this gap, our paper introduces a freely available, interactive liquidity stress-testing toolkit 2 for assessing Basel III liquidity coverage ratio-type shocks at the bank and economy level. It covers nearly 13,000 commercial banks across more than 100 economies since 2006, and incorporates pre-calibrated benchmark scenarios, pre-run simulations, and user-defined scenario options. An innovative “breakeven stress factor”—the minimum shock intensity at which a bank’s net liquidity turns negative—is the central output metric. Using the tool, we find meaningful cross-country heterogeneity in liquidity resilience and persistent rank ordering over time. We also discuss how rising run-off rates in a digitalised world and growing NBFI linkages challenge existing frameworks.
title: Ready-to-run global liquidity stress tests for banks and banking systems

abstract: Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is becoming a strategic component of aviation decarbonization, but its expansion depends on technological, economic, institutional, and resource conditions. This study compares the combinations of policy instruments, structural production characteristics, and market-governance arrangements observed in the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, Singapore, and Brazil, and considers the potential strategic vulnerabilities these configurations suggest, particularly for the European Union. The comparative qualitative policy analysis draws on peer-reviewed literature, legislation, regulatory documents, and institutional sources, organized through a single four-part framework: policy-instrument mix; structural production conditions; market and governance conditions; and potential strategic vulnerabilities. The cases display different configurations. The European Union and the United Kingdom emphasize mandatory demand; the United States relies more heavily on producer incentives; Japan and Singapore emphasize coordination and supply security; and Brazil combines established biofuel capabilities with a developing SAF framework. These observations do not identify causal effects or rank the configurations. Instead, they indicate possible exposure to feedstock, production, finance, policy-continuity, import, and certification constraints. Book-and-Claim is examined as a governance arrangement that separates environmental attributes from physical fuel flows; its practical contribution depends on credible certification, verification, registry governance, and interoperability. For the European Union, the comparison suggests that regulatory leadership may coexist with external supply and institutional dependencies. The concept of resilient interdependence is therefore proposed as a policy lens rather than a measured outcome.
title: The emerging geopolitics of sustainable aviation fuel: Policy architectures, book-and-claim and european strategic dependencies

abstract: This review examines how virtual embodiment interventions can inform economic research on inequality across social groups. In these interventions, widely used in psychology and related disciplines, virtual reality is used to embody individuals in virtual bodies whose appearance (skin tone, gender, age, etc.) can be experimentally manipulated to represent a member of a distinct social group. We propose a simple framework for understanding how outgroup embodiment may affect prejudice- and identity-related outcomes through other-regarding preferences, beliefs about the represented group, and beliefs about the self. We synthesize the existing literature, provide a practical guide to designing such interventions, and discuss the methodological trade-offs involved in their implementation. The review makes a two-way contribution: embodiment interventions offer economists a promising tool to study the socio-cognitive foundations of inequality, while an economic framework provides a path toward clarifying whether “changing bodies” can change not only minds but also behavior.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
source_issue: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 252
title: Changing bodies changes minds—and behavior? An economist’s guide to embodiment interventions

abstract: We study the impact of India’s National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (NREGS) on household borrowing from banks. Exploiting the program’s staggered rollout, we find a significant increase in personal loans and bank accounts in the early-adopting districts. Using household-level data, we show that NREGS-participating households had higher confidence in banks and were more likely to borrow from banks than from moneylenders. These effects are strongest among households with the highest NREGS earnings. Banks were also more likely to approve loan applications from NREGS-participating households, suggesting that these households became better credit risks, possibly because the program provided an income floor and reduced information asymmetries. This paper provides evidence on the interactions between welfare and credit markets within the context of a large developing country. More broadly, our findings suggest that investments in state capacity (the state’s ability to design, implement, and enforce policies) support financial market development.
title: Banking on jobs: Impact of a workfare program on formal credit

abstract: Large infrastructure investments, such as railroads, in migrant-sending countries can reduce emigration costs and increase local development, with ambiguous effects on net emigration rates. This column examines how the construction of Mexico’s railroad network between 1880 and 1910 shaped migration to the US over more than a century. Railroad access raised emigration rates to the US about fourfold in the early 1900s, mainly by allowing people to migrate in steps, which relaxed credit constraints on international migration. A century later, long after railroads became obsolete, locations with historical access to railroads send fewer migrants, but they still send them to the same US destination. Railroads created self-reinforcing migration corridors that outlasted the infrastructure itself.
title: The short- and long-run effects of railroads on Mexico–US migration

abstract: Every institution in modern finance exists to manufacture and maintain trust across society. This column argues that artificial intelligence poses new threats to trust which can fundamentally endanger the financial system. Deepfakes and voice cloning make it hard to verify identity or trust visual and audio evidence. A further threat is asymmetric understanding, where AI agents act on decision rules and representations of the world that humans cannot interpret or audit. Policy must adapt to preserve accountability, build resilience against AI-enabled fraud, and protect institutional trust.
title: Trust beyond face-to-face contact: AI and the future of finance

abstract: 链长制是提升产业链韧性的重要地方政策创新,厘清其对绿色创新的赋能效应,有助于推动产业与环境政策协同落地。本文基于各地链长制政策文本与链主企业名录,运用双重差分法考察链长制对企业绿色创新的影响。研究发现,链长制显著促进企业绿色创新,该效应在供应链集中度较高、规模较大以及制造业企业中尤为突出。机制分析表明,链长通过将绿色目标纳入产业链发展规划,缓解企业资金与技术瓶颈推动绿色创新;市场链主通过增强供应链气候风险感知,发挥链主知识溢出与示范引领作用驱动绿色创新。进一步分析发现,链长制与绿色政策可协同促进绿色创新。本研究揭示了链长制赋能绿色创新的政企协同路径,为复杂经济环境下产业政策优化与绿色转型提供参考。

abstract: 企业数智化转型是实现新型工业化和高质量发展的必然选择。本文基于2015-2023年沪深A股上市公司数据,运用关键词辅助主题模型测度企业数智化转型水平,并结合文本分析方法从政府采购合同大数据中识别政府数智采购合同。双重机器学习等估计结果表明政府数智采购显著促进了企业数智化转型,提升管理层数智化注意力配置、促进数智人力资本积累和缓解融资约束是重要的中介渠道。因果机器学习分析显示,政府数智采购对企业数智化的提升存在很大的分化,9%的企业并未从中受益;企业规模、采购流程数字化、地方保护主义是重要的异质性来源。进一步分析发现,政府数智采购与政府数智补贴、税收优惠之间存在协同效应。本文的研究结论凸显了政府数智采购作为市场型政策工具的重要价值,为进一步优化需求侧政策以推动企业数智化转型提供了有益借鉴。

abstract: 以强化产业链为导向的产业链政策,正深刻推动地方招商模式转型与现代化产业体系建设。本文基于2011-2023年工商企业注册数据,结合手工整理的地方“链长制”实施信息,采用多期双重差分方法,考察链长制对城市-行业层面企业进入及在位企业发展的影响。研究发现,链长制显著促进了政策目标产业链所属行业及其上游企业进入,有助于推进建链、补链、延链。地方政府发挥链长的统筹协调职能,通过定向配置土地资源为相关企业进入提供要素保障,并在缺乏“链主企业”时发挥更强的政策补位作用。链长制能够显著提升链内重点企业的全要素生产率和产能利用率,扩大其经营规模,并降低其管理费用;但企业研发投入强度和固定资产投入强度并未同步提高,且金融资产占比有所上升,强链举措尚未充分促进链内重点企业长期创新和实体资本积累。本研究为优化地方产业链治理和推进现代化产业体系建设提供了经验证据和决策参考。

abstract: 在数字经济重塑要素结构背景下,研发税收激励能否推动企业数字资本深化,是评估财税制度的重要问题。以2016年研发费用加计扣除政策为准自然实验,采用双重差分法发现,该政策提高了企业单位劳动所配置的数字资本,源于数字无形资产增加和员工规模下降,而非数字资本总量扩张,对传统资本深化影响不显著。机制上,人力资本升级、数字化行为和融资摩擦缓解是主要渠道。进一步,劳动端效率与分配改善,资本端投资不足缓解,但数字资本产出率和全要素生产率未显著提升;传统资本深化能增强政策的全要素生产率效应,数字资本深化作用不显著,呈现“要素配置调整先行、效率改善尚未显现”特征。本文揭示数字资本深化与生产率改善的非同步性,并从互补性投入视角对此进行了解释。

abstract: 在构建优质高效服务业新体系的背景下,如何释放受空间可达性限制的服务业发展潜力,成为扩大内需的关键。本文利用滴滴出行分批获得经营许可证的准自然实验,系统评估了网约车平台市场准入对消费性服务业扩张的影响。研究发现：第一,网约车平台市场准入显著提升了零售、餐饮、住宿和娱乐业的新注册企业数量,同时提升了在位企业营业收入;第二,其效应源于消费者出行便利性提升激发的潜在消费需求,表现为中高收入家庭外出消费增加和无车家庭的文化娱乐服务消费增加;第三,网约车平台市场准入改变消费性服务业进入的空间布局,新注册企业集中在距区县中心2-4公里范围内,且未导致城市公共交通供给规模显著收缩。本文为理解数字经济背景下共享出行平台市场准入如何通过重塑空间可达性释放服务消费潜力、促进服务业高质量发展,提供了关键经验证据。

abstract: 人口结构变化如何重塑产业结构,是理解后人口转变时期经济结构演进的重要议题。本文构建包含制造业、养老服务业与非养老服务业的多部门世代交叠模型,考察以预期寿命延长和生育率下降为特征的人口结构变化对产业结构的影响。研究发现：第一,预期寿命延长主要通过储蓄-投资渠道提高资本积累和投资品需求,进而提升制造业名义产出占比;生育率下降则通过改变年龄结构和不同年龄群体的消费需求份额,影响服务业内部结构。第二,人口结构变化引致的劳动力短缺不会导致制造业萎缩,自动化替代能够缓解劳动力供给收缩带来的产出冲击。第三,养老服务刚性需求通过提高家庭预防性储蓄和社会养老服务需求,带动制造业与养老服务业产出增长。第四,延迟退休和养老服务价格补贴能够缓解家庭预算约束,释放消费需求并促进服务业发展。本文拓展了人口转变视角下的结构转型研究。

abstract: 青少年体育锻炼的长期劳动力市场回报是人力资本研究的前沿议题。本文基于中国家庭追踪调查微观数据,运用队列双重差分模型考察青少年体育锻炼对个体成年工资性收入的影响。研究发现,青少年持续体育锻炼可显著提升成年收入水平,且锻炼起始年龄越早、社区体育设施供给越完善,收入回报越高。机制检验证实,体育锻炼主要通过培育非认知能力、优化职业选择、提升工作能力促进收入增长,认知能力与受教育程度并非核心渠道。此外,成本收益分析表明,青少年早期体育干预具有重要的经济社会价值。本文揭示了体育锻炼经由非认知能力路径实现长期回报的因果机制,为早期“投资于人”的政策提供了微观证据。

abstract: Carbon inequality is an important dimension of climate justice because high-emission groups and climate-vulnerable groups are often not the same. If excessive emissions among high-income groups are not effectively reduced, mitigation burdens may shift toward lower-income groups whose emissions are largely tied to basic needs, leaving little room for further emission reductions. We examine whether gender equality reduces carbon inequality and through what mechanisms using a theoretical model and panel data for 153 countries from 2006 to 2019. We find that gender equality significantly mitigates carbon inequality by reducing income and wealth inequality, with stronger effects under greater democratization and lower corruption. The reduction in carbon inequality is driven mainly by lower emissions among high-emission groups, while the direct effects on low-emission groups are limited. These findings link gender equality to the structure of carbon emissions and highlight the roles of redistribution, social inclusion, and quality of governance in promoting climate justice.
title: Gender Equality and Carbon Inequality: Do Social Ideologies Matter?

abstract: We study how the demand for programming skills has impacted inequality. We create a new dataset with information on wages, employment, and software of Brazilian programmers, covering the period from the birth of information technology (IT) to the rise of artificial intelligence (AI). High-ability, high-wage, and highly educated individuals in key technology hubs are more likely to become programmers. Creating software is associated with higher wages and better career prospects for programmers, especially for those with specialized skills in AI and cybersecurity. These wage gains are concentrated among top programmers, increasing inequality within the profession. Therefore, increased demand for specialized skills in programming has contributed to wage inequality both within the programming field and between programmers and other occupations.
title: How demand for new skills affects wage inequality: The case of software programmers

abstract: We quantify how the gender wage gap emerges over the working life across 29 European countries using a life-cycle accounting approach. The framework separates the gender wage gap already present before first childbirth from a childbirth-related component and a post-childbirth-related component. The pre-childbirth component accounts for a large share of the gap in Central and Eastern as well as Southern European countries, while the childbirth-related component is by far the largest in Northern and Western European ones. We complement these findings using an alternative approach that relates the gender wage gap directly to worker, job and firm characteristics. The complementary proximate-characteristics approach shows that part-time work accounts for a substantial share of the gender wage gap in Northern and Western European countries, whereas a larger share remains unexplained by the observed worker, job and firm characteristics in Central and Eastern and Southern European countries. Although the results are descriptive rather than identifying causal mechanisms, they nonetheless suggest that further prioritising family policies and encouraging wider acceptance of flexible work schedules are particularly relevant in Northern and Western Europe. In Central and Eastern as well as Southern Europe, anti-discrimination policies and measures addressing gender stereotypes may also remain relevant.
title: Accounting for the gender wage gap in 29 European countries

abstract: Earth observation (EO) data can help advance our understanding of drivers of agricultural productivity, as well as the complex relationships between this productivity and natural resources, conflict, and climate change. This special issue provides a wide range of papers highlighting some of the benefits–and challenges–of integrating EO data into impact studies in these contexts. EO can provide objective estimates of cereal crop productivity, land use, environmental conditions, and some agricultural practices. The high frequency and long time series of EO data can also enable observation of state-dependent impacts, as well as longer-term dynamics. The wide geographic coverage of EO data further allows direct observation of spatial spillovers–including environmental harms or improvements–and can provide data from fragile or conflict-affected settings where collecting ground data may not be feasible. The papers in the issue also show, however, that EO data introduce their own set of challenges, ranging from measurement error to interpretation. The papers together demonstrate that EO data are best used in combination with ground-based data, careful analysis of mechanisms, and transparent discussion of their limitations. The papers also point to many future research directions in both leveraging EO data and addressing those limitations.
title: Introduction to Special Issue: Integrating Earth Observation into Impact Studies in Agriculture and Climate Change

abstract: This study examines whether pluralistic teaching is associated with students’ learning dispositions. The data are drawn from an economic inequality course delivered at an English university between 2016 and 2025. A new scale capturing pluralistic knowledge of economic inequality is developed around six principles: structural and relational ontology; epistemic pluralism and situated knowledge; intersectional and decolonial analysis; normative commitment to justice, equity and transformation; methodological diversity and grounded inquiry; and engaged scholarship and evidence-informed policymaking. The results show that, after completing the course, students reported higher levels of pluralistic knowledge of economic inequality and stronger learning dispositions relating to critical thinking, epistemic curiosity, civic engagement, self-efficacy and social justice. Pluralistic knowledge of economic inequality is also positively associated with these learning dispositions. In addition, both pluralistic knowledge and learning dispositions are positively associated with academic performance in course assessments.
title: Teaching Economic Inequality: Pluralistic Knowledge and Learning Dispositions

abstract: This paper examines competitive information disclosure in search markets with a mix of selective consumers, who search costlessly, and casual consumers, who incur positive search costs. Selective consumers incentivize truthful disclosure; casual consumers, concealment. With both types, the equilibrium features partial disclosure, which persists despite intense competition.
title: Limits of Disclosure in Search Markets

abstract: Does competition always mitigate the impact of discrimination on racial wage gaps? This paper examines the impact of product market competition on customer-driven taste-based discrimination in a service economy characterized by homophily. I develop a novel equilibrium model of both product and labor markets in which heightened product market competition tends to exacerbate labor market discrimination in customer-facing occupations.
title: Is the Customer Always Right? Customer Taste-Based Discrimination and Competition
